topics.ch: Building Blocks in Economics: The Problem of Choice
topics.h: The school canteen has 50 hot samosas at break time and 120 hungry students in the queue. Who gets one? Welcome to economics!
p: Human wants are unlimited: as soon as one want is satisfied, new wants appear.
Resources such as land, water, workers, machines, money and time are limited, and most of them can be put to more than one use.
Scarcity means that resources are limited compared with our wants. Because of scarcity, every person, family, business and country has to make choices.
Economic goods are scarce and usually carry a price, like rice, petrol or a notebook. Free goods, like the air we breathe, are available in plenty and cost nothing.
Goods and services are made using four factors of production: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. Their rewards are rent, wages, interest and profit.

ex.q: Think it through: A very rich businesswoman in Mumbai can buy almost anything she likes. Does she face scarcity too?
st: Scarcity is not the same as being poor. It means resources are limited compared with wants.
She still has only 24 hours in a day, so she must choose between a meeting, time with family and rest.
Her money is large but still limited compared with all the things she could want, so she must choose between projects too.
So scarcity touches everyone, rich or poor, and everyone has to make choices.
ex.a: Yes. Her time and even her money are limited compared with her wants, so she must also choose.

topics.rl: Limited train seats during Diwali, water tankers shared by a colony in summer, and your own 24 hours split between study, play and sleep are all examples of scarcity.

rv.summary: Human wants are unlimited, but resources like land, labour, money and time are limited and have alternative uses. This scarcity forces everyone, rich or poor, to make choices.
focus: Explain scarcity as limited resources compared with wants
Tell free goods from economic goods
Name the four factors of production and their rewards
Why resources with alternative uses force choices
remember: Scarcity: resources are limited compared with our wants
Free goods (like air) are plentiful and cost nothing; economic goods are scarce and carry a price
Factors and rewards: land–rent, labour–wages, capital–interest, entrepreneurship–profit
Capital: man-made goods such as machines, tools and buildings used to produce other goods
traps: Scarcity is not the same as being poor or a good being unavailable
Don't reverse it: wants are unlimited, resources are limited
A tractor is capital, not land

topics.ch: Building Blocks in Economics: The Problem of Choice
topics.t: Opportunity cost: the price of a choice
topics.h: You choose to watch a cricket final instead of going to your friend's birthday party. The match was free. Or was it?
p: Every choice has a cost, because choosing one option means giving up others.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made. Only the next best option counts, not all the options together.
Opportunity cost is not always money. It can be time, fun, rest or a chance to learn something.
Good decisions compare the benefit of an option with its opportunity cost.

A production possibility curve shows the combinations of two goods an economy can make with its resources and technology. To make more of one good, it must make less of the other, and the amount given up is the opportunity cost.

ex.q: Think it through: Arjun has a free Sunday evening. In order of his liking, he could study for Monday's test, play cricket with friends or watch a film. He chooses to study. What is his opportunity cost?
st: List the options he did not choose: cricket and the film.
Find the next best of these. Cricket was his second choice.
Opportunity cost counts only the next best alternative, so the film is not added.
So the cost of studying is the cricket game he gave up.
ex.a: The game of cricket with his friends, his next best alternative.

topics.rl: When your family spends savings on a new fridge instead of a holiday, or when a city uses land for a metro depot instead of a park, the option given up is the opportunity cost.

rv.summary: Every choice has a cost because choosing one option means giving up others. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, and it can be time, fun or rest, not only money.
focus: Find the opportunity cost from a ranked list of options
Work out opportunity cost in rupees or units given up
Explain that 'free' things still have an opportunity cost
Read a production possibility choice: more of one good means less of the other
remember: Opportunity cost: value of the next best alternative given up
Only the next best option counts, not all options together
On a production possibility curve, the amount of one good given up to make more of the other is the opportunity cost
traps: Don't add up all the options given up; take only the next best
Opportunity cost is not always money; it can be time
Don't give the value of the chosen option as the opportunity cost

topics.ch: Building Blocks in Economics: The Problem of Choice
topics.h: Should India grow more rice or more cotton? Use more machines or more workers? And who gets what is made? Every country must answer these questions.
p: Because of scarcity, every economy, from a family to a whole country, faces three central problems.
What to produce and how much: which goods and services to make with limited resources, for example more food grains or more cars, more schools or more roads.
How to produce: which technique to use. A labour-intensive technique uses more workers, while a capital-intensive technique uses more machines.
For whom to produce: how the goods and services, and the incomes earned, are shared among people.

In a market economy, buyers and sellers solve these problems through prices. In a centrally planned (command) economy, the government decides. A mixed economy, like India, uses both markets and government.

ex.q: Think it through: A women's self-help group in an Odisha village has ₹50,000 and 10 members. Which central problems must it solve?
st: What to produce: should they make pickles, papads or both, and how many packets?
How to produce: should they make them by hand (more labour) or buy a machine (more capital)?
For whom to produce: who will buy the products, and how will the earnings be shared among the 10 members?
These are the same three questions a whole country faces, only on a smaller scale.
ex.a: What to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.

topics.rl: When your family decides what to cook, whether to grind spices at home or buy them ready-made, and how to share the food, it is solving its own small 'central problems'.

rv.summary: Because of scarcity, every economy faces three central problems: what to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce. Markets solve them through prices, a command economy through the government, and a mixed economy like India uses both.
focus: Identify which central problem a given decision belongs to
Tell labour-intensive from capital-intensive techniques
How market, command and mixed economies solve the problems
Why the central problems arise
remember: Three central problems: what to produce, how to produce, for whom to produce
Labour-intensive: more workers; capital-intensive: more machines
Market economy: prices; command economy: government decides; mixed economy (India): both
traps: Don't confuse 'how to produce' (technique) with 'what to produce' (goods)
'For whom' is about sharing output and incomes, not choosing the product
India is neither purely market nor purely command; it is mixed

topics.ch: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topics.t: Demand and the law of demand
topics.h: When mangoes first arrive in May they are costly, and your family buys just a few. By June the price drops and suddenly there are mangoes in every bag. That is demand at work!
p: Demand is the quantity of a good that buyers are willing and able to buy at a given price during a period of time. Wanting something without the money to pay for it is not demand.

Law of demand: other things remaining the same, when the price of a good rises, its quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, the quantity demanded rises. Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.
A demand schedule is a table of prices and quantities demanded. Drawn on a graph, it gives a demand curve that slopes downward from left to right.
Besides its own price, demand also depends on buyers' income, prices of related goods, tastes and season, and what buyers expect about future prices.
Related goods can be substitutes, used in place of each other (tea and coffee), or complements, used together (cricket bat and ball).

ex.q: Think it through: In a Lucknow fruit market, buyers purchase 10 kg of mangoes a day at ₹100 per kg, 20 kg at ₹80, 35 kg at ₹60 and 50 kg at ₹40. What does this schedule show?
st: As the price falls from ₹100 to ₹40 per kg, the quantity bought rises from 10 kg to 50 kg.
Price and quantity demanded are moving in opposite directions.
A lower price makes mangoes more affordable and makes them a better deal compared with other fruits, so people buy more.
This is exactly what the law of demand predicts.
ex.a: It shows the law of demand: as the price falls, the quantity demanded rises.

topics.rl: Big festival sales, cheaper vegetables at the end of the day in a mandi, and people buying more train tickets when fares are cut all show the law of demand.

rv.summary: Demand is the quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at a price. By the law of demand, other things being equal, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so the demand curve slopes downward.
focus: State the law of demand and read a demand schedule
Tell demand apart from a mere desire
Effects of substitutes and complements
Other factors that change demand: income, season, tastes, expected prices
remember: Demand: quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at a given price during a period
Law of demand: price up → quantity demanded down; price down → quantity demanded up (other things the same)
Demand curve slopes downward from left to right
Substitutes: tea and coffee. Complements: cricket bat and ball.
traps: Wanting something without the ability to pay is not demand
Don't mix up the demand curve (downward) with the supply curve (upward)
Don't treat complements like substitutes

topics.ch: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topics.t: Supply and the law of supply
topics.h: Just before Diwali, a potter in Kutch works late every night making diyas. Why does he make so many more now than in March?
p: Supply is the quantity of a good that sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price during a period of time.

Law of supply: other things remaining the same, when the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, and when the price falls, the quantity supplied falls. Price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.
Sellers offer more at higher prices because they can earn more profit and can cover the extra cost of making more. So a supply curve slopes upward from left to right.
Supply also depends on the cost of inputs (seeds, fuel, wages), technology, weather for farm goods, the number of sellers, and taxes or subsidies.
Stock is the total quantity a seller has. Supply is only the part of that stock offered for sale at a particular price.

ex.q: Think it through: A potter offers 100 diyas a day when the price is ₹5 each, 200 at ₹10, 250 at ₹15 and 300 at ₹20. What does this show?
st: As the price rises from ₹5 to ₹20, the quantity offered rises from 100 to 300 diyas.
Price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.
A higher price means more earnings for each diya, so it is worth his extra time, clay and fuel.
This matches the law of supply.
ex.a: It shows the law of supply: as the price rises, the quantity supplied rises.

topics.rl: When onion prices shoot up, farmers plan to grow more onions next season. When cold storage or better seeds become available, the supply of potatoes rises.

rv.summary: Supply is the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at a price. By the law of supply, other things being equal, price and quantity supplied move in the same direction, so the supply curve slopes upward.
focus: State the law of supply and read a supply schedule
Why sellers offer more at higher prices
Factors that change supply: input costs, technology, weather, number of sellers, taxes and subsidies
Tell stock apart from supply
remember: Supply: quantity sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price during a period
Law of supply: price up → quantity supplied up (other things the same)
Supply curve slopes upward from left to right
Stock is the total a seller has; supply is the part offered for sale at a price
traps: Don't confuse stock with supply
Higher input costs reduce supply; better technology increases it
Don't mix up the law of supply with the law of demand

topics.ch: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topics.t: Market equilibrium: where demand meets supply
topics.h: Nobody in the sabzi mandi announces the price of tomatoes on a loudspeaker, yet by mid-morning almost everyone is paying about the same price. Who decided it?
p: The market price is set by the meeting of demand (buyers) and supply (sellers).
Equilibrium price is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At this price the market 'clears': there is no extra unsold stock and no buyer left unable to buy at that price.
If the price is above equilibrium, quantity supplied is more than quantity demanded. This surplus (excess supply) pushes sellers to cut the price.
If the price is below equilibrium, quantity demanded is more than quantity supplied. This shortage (excess demand) pushes the price up.
When demand rises (for example, sweets at Diwali) the equilibrium price rises. When supply rises (for example, a bumper harvest) the equilibrium price falls.

ex.q: Think it through: Tomatoes in a mandi. At ₹20 per kg, buyers want 100 kg and sellers offer 40 kg. At ₹30: 80 kg and 60 kg. At ₹40: 60 kg and 60 kg. At ₹50: 40 kg and 80 kg. Find the equilibrium.
st: Look for the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
At ₹40 per kg, both are 60 kg.
At ₹20 or ₹30 there is a shortage, so the price would be pushed up.
At ₹50 there is a surplus of 80 − 40 = 40 kg, so sellers would cut the price.
ex.a: The equilibrium price is ₹40 per kg and the equilibrium quantity is 60 kg.

topics.rl: Flower prices jump before festivals and weddings, while vegetable prices drop after a good harvest. In each case demand and supply move the price.

rv.summary: The market price is set where demand meets supply. At the equilibrium price, quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. A price above it causes a surplus that pushes the price down; a price below it causes a shortage that pushes the price up.
focus: Find the equilibrium price and quantity from a schedule
Surplus above equilibrium, shortage below it, and their effect on price
Calculate the size of a surplus or shortage
Effect of a rise in demand or in supply on the equilibrium price
remember: Equilibrium price: quantity demanded = quantity supplied
Above equilibrium: surplus (excess supply) → price falls
Below equilibrium: shortage (excess demand) → price rises
Demand rises → price rises. Supply rises → price falls.
traps: Don't mix up surplus and shortage
More supply with the same demand lowers the price; it does not raise it
Surplus = quantity supplied − quantity demanded; don't add them

topics.h: Your pocket money is gone by the 10th of every month, and you cannot remember where it went. A budget is the detective that finds out!
p: A budget is a plan of expected income and spending for a period such as a week, a month or a year.
Income is the money coming in, such as a salary, pocket money, business profit or interest. Expenses are the money going out.

Fixed expenses stay about the same each month (rent, school fees, a loan instalment). Variable expenses change (groceries, electricity, outings). Needs, such as food, shelter, medicines and education, come before wants.
If income is more than expenses, the budget has a surplus. If expenses are more than income, it has a deficit. If the two are equal, it is balanced.
'Pay yourself first': set aside savings as soon as money comes in, then spend the rest. Tracking every expense shows where money leaks away.

ex.q: Think it through: The Sharma family in Jaipur earns ₹40,000 a month. They spend ₹12,000 on rent, ₹9,000 on groceries, ₹5,000 on school fees, ₹2,500 on electricity and phone, ₹3,000 on travel and ₹2,500 on outings. Is their budget in surplus or deficit?
st: Compare with income: ₹40,000 − ₹34,000 = ₹6,000.
Income is more than expenses, so the budget has a surplus.
The family can save the ₹6,000 or keep part of it for emergencies.

topics.rl: Families plan monthly household budgets, schools plan for annual functions, and the Government of India presents a budget in Parliament every year.

rv.summary: A budget plans expected income and spending for a period. Income more than expenses is a surplus, less is a deficit, and equal is balanced. Put needs before wants, save first and track every expense.
focus: Calculate surplus, deficit or money left from a budget
Tell fixed expenses from variable expenses
Tell needs from wants
Explain 'pay yourself first' and why tracking expenses helps
remember: Budget: a plan of expected income and spending for a period
Surplus = income − expenses (when income is more); deficit when expenses are more; balanced when equal
Fixed: rent, school fees, loan instalment. Variable: groceries, electricity, outings.
Pay yourself first: set aside savings as soon as money comes in
traps: Don't mix up surplus and deficit
An essential expense is not always fixed; electricity use changes month to month
Don't give total spending when asked how much is left

topics.h: Put ₹1,000 in a bank and do nothing. A year later there is more than ₹1,000. Where did the extra money come from?
p: Saving means keeping aside the part of income that is not spent today, for goals such as education, a bicycle or emergencies. An emergency fund is money kept ready for sudden needs like illness or repairs.
Banks keep savings safe and pay interest. A savings account lets you take money out any time. A fixed deposit locks money for a fixed period and usually pays a higher rate of interest.
Simple interest is paid only on the original amount (the principal): Simple interest = Principal × Rate × Time ÷ 100.
Compound interest is paid on the principal plus the interest already earned, so money grows faster over time. Starting to save early gives compounding more time to work.
Inflation is a general rise in prices over time. It lowers the purchasing power of money, so savings should ideally grow faster than prices rise.

ex.q: Think it through: Isha puts ₹5,000 in a bank at 10% interest a year for 2 years. How much interest does she earn with simple interest, and with interest compounded yearly?
st: Compound interest, year 1: 10% of ₹5,000 = ₹500, so she has ₹5,500.
Year 2: 10% of ₹5,500 = ₹550, so she has ₹6,050. Total interest = ₹1,050.
Compound interest gives ₹50 more because in year 2 she also earns interest on the first year's interest.

topics.rl: A piggy bank keeps coins safe but adds nothing, while a bank savings account or a recurring deposit, which many parents open for children's goals, earns interest.

rv.summary: Saving keeps aside unspent income for goals and emergencies. Banks pay interest: simple interest only on the principal, compound interest also on earlier interest, so starting early helps. Inflation lowers the purchasing power of money.

Explain why compound interest grows faster and why starting early helps
Savings account vs fixed deposit, and the purpose of an emergency fund
Effect of inflation on prices and purchasing power

Compound interest: interest is earned on principal plus interest already earned
Fixed deposit: money locked for a fixed period, usually higher interest
Inflation: a general rise in prices; it lowers the purchasing power of money
traps: Don't forget to divide by 100 or multiply by time in simple interest
Don't use simple interest when the question says compounded yearly
Higher prices make money worth less, not more

topics.t: Financial literacy: borrowing, risk and staying safe
topics.h: "Congratulations! You have won ₹50,000. Just share the OTP sent to your phone." Would you share it? A financially smart person never would!
p: Financial literacy means having the knowledge and skills to earn, spend, save, borrow and invest money wisely.

A loan must be repaid with interest. Banks are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), and formal lenders such as banks and cooperatives usually charge lower interest than informal moneylenders. Borrow only what you can repay.
Higher returns usually come with higher risk. Spreading savings across different options (diversification) reduces risk: don't put all your eggs in one basket.
Insurance protects against big losses. You pay a small regular amount (premium), and the insurer pays if the insured loss, such as illness or crop damage, happens.

Stay safe: never share your OTP, PIN, CVV or passwords; banks never ask for them. You do not need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money. Offers that promise to double money quickly are likely frauds. Report cyber fraud on the national helpline 1930.

ex.q: Think it through: Rohan gets an SMS: "You have won a lottery of ₹50,000! Click this link and share the OTP to claim it." He never bought a lottery ticket. What should he do?
st: He did not enter any lottery, so the 'prize' cannot be real.
An OTP is a secret code that lets someone approve a transaction from his account. Sharing it could let a fraudster take his money.
He should not click the link or share the OTP, and should delete the message.
He should tell a parent and, if any money is lost, report it quickly on the cyber fraud helpline 1930.
ex.a: Ignore the message, never share the OTP or click the link, tell an adult and report fraud on 1930 if needed.

topics.rl: Families compare loan interest rates before buying a scooter, farmers buy crop insurance before the sowing season, and shopkeepers check payment messages before handing over goods.

rv.summary: Financial literacy means using money wisely. Borrow only what you can repay, prefer RBI-regulated lenders, diversify to reduce risk and use insurance against big losses. Never share OTP, PIN, CVV or passwords, and report cyber fraud on 1930.

topics.h: Every summer, a family in a Himachal village watched extra plums rot under the trees. Their daughter saw something different: a chance to make jam. That is how an entrepreneur thinks!
p: An entrepreneur is a person who spots an opportunity, often a problem people face, and starts an enterprise to meet it.
The entrepreneur brings together the other factors of production (land, labour and capital), makes the key decisions and bears the risk. The reward is profit, but there can also be a loss.
Useful qualities include creativity, willingness to take calculated risks, decision-making, leadership and persistence, which means learning from failure and trying again.
Some entrepreneurs run small local businesses, some build fast-growing startups, and social entrepreneurs start ventures mainly to solve a social problem, such as clean water or low-cost learning.
Entrepreneurs create jobs, bring new products and services, raise incomes and help the economy grow. They become job creators, not only job seekers.

ex.q: Think it through: Anjali sees that plums in her village rot every season. She uses her savings to buy jars and a stove, rents a small room, hires two helpers and sells plum jam in nearby towns. Where do you see entrepreneurship?
st: Opportunity: she turned a problem (wasted fruit) into a product people would buy.
Organising: she combined land (the rented room), labour (two helpers) and capital (stove and jars).
Risk: her own savings are at stake, and she could make a loss if the jam does not sell.
Reward: if customers like the jam, she earns a profit and creates jobs in the village.
ex.a: Anjali spotted an opportunity, organised resources, took the risk and aims to earn a profit, so she is an entrepreneur.

topics.rl: The neighbourhood tiffin service, the tailor who starts a small garment unit and a young engineer who builds an app for farmers are all entrepreneurs.

rv.summary: An entrepreneur spots an opportunity, brings together land, labour and capital, makes key decisions and bears the risk, earning profit or facing a loss. Entrepreneurs create jobs and help the economy grow.

topics.h: Most great startups begin with someone saying, "Why is this so difficult? There must be a better way!"
p: A startup is a young business built around a new or improved idea that aims to grow quickly and serve many customers.
It begins with a real problem. Talking to possible customers and studying the market (market research) tells you whether people truly need your solution.
Instead of building the perfect product at once, founders make a simple first version, a prototype or minimum viable product (MVP), test it with users, take feedback and improve it.
If feedback shows the plan is not working, founders may pivot, which means changing the product or the target customers.

A business plan explains the product, the customers, the costs, the price and the expected profit. Money can come from own savings (bootstrapping), family, bank loans, angel investors or venture capital firms. Investors usually get a share of ownership, called equity.

ex.q: Think it through: Zoya's startup sells cloth bags. Each bag costs ₹30 to make and sells for ₹50. She sells 200 bags in a month and pays ₹1,000 rent. What is her profit for the month?
st: Profit on one bag = ₹50 − ₹30 = ₹20.
Subtract the rent: ₹4,000 − ₹1,000 = ₹3,000.
A business plan uses such numbers to check whether an idea can pay for itself.

topics.rl: School science fairs, college incubation centres and app ideas tested with a small group of users first are all ways young founders try out ideas before growing.

rv.summary: A startup is a young business built on a new idea that aims to grow fast. Founders start from a real problem, do market research, build an MVP, take feedback and may pivot. Money can come from bootstrapping, family, banks, angel investors or venture capital.
focus: Steps from idea to startup: problem, market research, MVP, feedback, pivot
Calculate profit from price, cost and number sold
Sources of startup funding
Meaning of equity and angel investor
remember: MVP: a simple first version tested with users
Pivot: changing the product or target customers after feedback
Bootstrapping: funding from your own savings
Equity: a share of ownership given to investors
traps: Don't use total sales as profit; profit = revenue − costs
Equity is ownership, not a loan that earns interest

topics.h: A potter from Gujarat, Mansukhbhai Prajapati, made a clay fridge called Mitticool that keeps food cool without electricity. Innovation can come from anyone, anywhere!
p: An invention is the creation of something new. Innovation is putting a new or better idea to practical use, as a product, a process or a way of serving customers.
Frugal innovation means creating useful, low-cost solutions with limited resources, like a clay fridge that runs without electricity.

Ideas can be protected by law: a patent protects a new invention (for 20 years in India), a trademark protects a brand name or logo, and copyright protects creative work such as books, music and software.

The Government of India launched the Startup India initiative on 16 January 2016 to support new businesses. Incubators and accelerators help startups with mentoring, workspace and contacts, and Atal Tinkering Labs let school students build and test ideas.
A startup valued at US$1 billion or more is called a unicorn. Many startups fail, and founders treat failure as a lesson.

ex.q: Think it through: An engineer designs a solar dryer. Later, a startup in Maharashtra makes it cheaply and sells it to onion farmers so they can dry and store their crop. Which part is invention and which is innovation?
st: Designing the new solar dryer is the invention: something new has been created.
Making it affordable and bringing it to farmers who use it is the innovation: the idea is put to practical use.
The farmers gain because less of their crop is wasted.
So innovation turns a good idea into real value for people.
ex.a: Designing the dryer is invention. Making and selling it for farmers to use is innovation.

topics.rl: Paying a vegetable seller by scanning a QR code, booking a doctor's appointment on an app and using a low-cost water filter in a village are everyday results of innovation.

rv.summary: Invention creates something new; innovation puts ideas to practical use, and frugal innovation does it at low cost. Patents, trademarks and copyright protect ideas. Startup India (16 January 2016), incubators and Atal Tinkering Labs support new ventures.

qa.q: What is the basic economic problem that every society faces?
qa.a: Wants are unlimited but resources are limited
qa.e: Economics begins with scarcity: our wants keep growing, but the resources to satisfy them are limited, so we must choose.

qa.q: Which of these is a free good?
qa.a: The air we breathe
qa.e: The air we breathe is available in plenty and nobody has to pay for it, so it is a free good. The others are scarce and have a price.

qa.q: In economics, what does 'scarcity' mean?
qa.a: Resources are limited compared with people's wants
qa.e: Scarcity is about limited resources compared with wants. Even goods sold in every shop are scarce in this sense, because they cannot be made in endless amounts.

qa.q: A farmer in Punjab uses a tractor to plough his field. Which factor of production is the tractor?
qa.a: Capital
qa.e: Capital means man-made goods, such as machines, tools and buildings, that are used to produce other goods. A tractor is capital.

qa.q: What is the reward earned by labour?
qa.a: Wages
qa.e: Workers earn wages (or salaries) for their physical and mental work. Rent goes to land, interest to capital and profit to the entrepreneur.

qa.q: A village has one empty plot of land. It could become a playground, a vegetable market or a health centre. What does this show?
qa.a: Resources have alternative uses
qa.e: The same resource can be used in different ways, but only one use can be chosen at a time. This is why choices are needed.

qa.q: Which statement about human wants is correct?
qa.a: When one want is satisfied, new wants usually arise
qa.e: Once Meera gets a bicycle, she may want a helmet, then a better bicycle. Wants keep coming back and growing, which is why they are called unlimited.

qa.q: Why does even a very rich person have to make choices?
qa.a: Time and other resources are still limited compared with wants
qa.e: Everyone has only 24 hours in a day, and even large resources are limited compared with wants. So scarcity, and the need to choose, affects everyone.

qa.q: What is opportunity cost?
qa.a: The value of the next best alternative given up
qa.e: Opportunity cost is what you sacrifice by choosing: the value of the next best option you could have had instead.

qa.q: Kavya can go to dance class, attend her cousin's birthday party or play badminton. She likes them in that order and goes to dance class. What is her opportunity cost?
qa.a: The birthday party
qa.e: Her next best option was the birthday party, so that is what she gave up. Badminton was only her third choice.

qa.q: A farmer's field can grow wheat worth ₹60,000, sugarcane worth ₹80,000 or vegetables worth ₹50,000 in a season. He grows sugarcane. What is his opportunity cost?
qa.e: Wheat at ₹60,000 is the best of the crops he did not grow, so it is the opportunity cost. We do not add the vegetables too.

qa.q: Sana spends two hours playing a mobile game instead of revising for her science test, which was her next best choice. What is the opportunity cost of the game?
qa.a: The two hours of revision she gave up
qa.e: Opportunity cost is not always money. Here it is the revision time, and the learning, that she gave up.

qa.q: A factory can make 6 cycles and 20 fans, or 4 cycles and 30 fans. If it moves from the first combination to the second, how many cycles is the opportunity cost of the extra 10 fans?
qa.e: To make 10 more fans, the factory gives up 6 − 4 = 2 cycles. Those 2 cycles are the opportunity cost.

qa.q: Rahul gets a free ticket to a three-hour film. Is watching the film really free for him?
qa.a: No, because he gives up the next best use of those three hours
qa.e: Even without paying money, he uses three hours that could have gone to something else he valued. That is the opportunity cost.

qa.q: A city council uses a plot of land to build a parking lot instead of a park, which was the next best option. What is the opportunity cost of the parking lot?
qa.a: The park that could have been built
qa.e: The park is the next best use of the land that was given up, so it is the opportunity cost.

qa.q: Why does opportunity cost exist?
qa.a: Because scarce resources force us to choose between options
qa.e: If resources were unlimited, we could have everything. Scarcity forces choices, and every choice means giving something up.

qa.q: A textile factory is deciding whether to use more machines or hire more workers. Which central problem is this?
qa.a: How to produce
qa.e: Choosing between more machines and more workers is a choice of technique, which is the problem of how to produce.

qa.q: A country must choose between producing more wheat or more cotton. Which central problem is this?
qa.a: What to produce
qa.e: Deciding which goods to make, and how much of each, is the problem of what to produce.

qa.q: The problem of 'for whom to produce' is about:
qa.a: How the output and incomes are shared among people
qa.e: 'For whom' deals with distribution: who gets the goods and services and how income is divided in society.

qa.q: Why do the central problems of an economy arise?
qa.a: Because resources are limited and have alternative uses
qa.e: If resources were unlimited, no choices would be needed. Scarcity of resources with alternative uses creates the central problems.

qa.q: A labour-intensive technique of production uses:
qa.a: More workers compared with machines
qa.e: Labour-intensive means relying more on human workers, like making handloom sarees, rather than heavy machinery.

qa.q: In a market economy, how are the central problems mainly solved?
qa.a: By buyers and sellers through the price mechanism
qa.e: In a market economy, prices set by demand and supply guide what is produced, how and for whom.

qa.q: What kind of economy does India have?
qa.a: A mixed economy
qa.e: India has a mixed economy: private businesses and markets work alongside the government, which runs some services such as railways and plans for public needs.

qa.q: In a centrally planned (command) economy, who mainly decides what, how and for whom to produce?
qa.a: The government
qa.e: In a centrally planned economy, a government authority plans and decides how resources are used.

qa.q: What does the law of demand state?
qa.a: Other things being equal, quantity demanded falls when price rises
qa.e: Under the law of demand, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, provided other factors stay the same.

qa.q: Ritu really wants a laptop but has no money and no way to pay for one. In economics, is this demand?
qa.a: No, because demand needs both the desire and the ability to pay
qa.e: Demand means being willing and able to buy at a price. A wish without the ability to pay is only a desire.

qa.q: The price of tea rises sharply. What is likely to happen to the demand for coffee?
qa.a: It rises
qa.e: Tea and coffee are substitutes. When tea becomes costly, some people switch to coffee, so demand for coffee rises.

qa.q: Cars and petrol are complements. If petrol becomes much more expensive, what is likely to happen to the demand for petrol cars?
qa.a: It falls
qa.e: Complements are used together. Costlier petrol makes running a petrol car more expensive, so fewer people want to buy one.

qa.q: When the price of mangoes falls from ₹80 to ₹40 per kg, the quantity demanded rises from 20 kg to 50 kg a day. By how much does the quantity demanded rise?
qa.a: 30 kg
qa.e: The rise is the new quantity minus the old one: 50 − 20 = 30 kg.

qa.q: The demand for umbrellas and raincoats goes up every July. Which factor explains this?
qa.a: Season and weather
qa.e: Demand depends on season and tastes, not just on price. In the monsoon more people need rain gear, even at the same price.

qa.q: How does a normal demand curve look on a graph?
qa.a: It slopes downward from left to right
qa.e: Because more is bought at lower prices, the curve falls from left to right.

qa.q: Why do economists say 'other things remaining the same' in the law of demand?
qa.a: To study the effect of price alone while income, tastes and other factors are held constant
qa.e: Many things affect demand. Holding them constant lets us see clearly how price by itself affects the quantity demanded.

qa.q: What does the law of supply state?
qa.a: Other things being equal, quantity supplied rises when price rises
qa.e: Under the law of supply, price and quantity supplied move in the same direction, as long as other factors stay the same.

qa.q: Which way does a normal supply curve slope?
qa.a: Upward from left to right
qa.e: Sellers offer more at higher prices, so the supply curve rises from left to right.

qa.q: A severe drought hits the onion-growing regions of Maharashtra. What happens to the supply of onions?
qa.a: It falls
qa.e: Farm output depends on weather. A drought means a smaller harvest, so fewer onions are available for sale.

qa.q: A new machine lets a brick kiln make bricks faster at a lower cost. What is likely to happen to the supply of bricks?
qa.a: It increases
qa.e: Better technology lowers the cost of production, so producers can offer more bricks at each price.

qa.q: A rice trader has 500 kg of rice in his godown. At today's price he offers 300 kg for sale. What is his supply of rice at this price?
qa.a: 300 kg
qa.e: Supply is only the quantity actually offered for sale at a given price, which is 300 kg. The 500 kg is his stock.

qa.q: When the price of a diya rises from ₹10 to ₹20, a potter increases his supply from 200 to 300 diyas a day. By how many diyas does supply rise?
qa.e: The rise in quantity supplied is 300 − 200 = 100 diyas a day.

qa.q: Why do sellers usually offer more of a good when its price rises?
qa.a: Because a higher price means more profit and covers the cost of producing more
qa.e: A higher price makes producing and selling more worthwhile, so sellers expand their output.

qa.q: The price of diesel for fishing boats in Kerala goes up a lot. What is likely to happen to the supply of fish?
qa.a: It falls
qa.e: Diesel is an input. When input costs rise, fishing becomes costlier, so less fish is offered at each price.

qa.q: What is the equilibrium price?
qa.a: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
qa.e: Equilibrium means balance. At this price, the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer.

qa.q: At ₹20 a dozen, buyers want 90 dozen bananas and sellers offer 30. At ₹30, buyers want 60 and sellers offer 60. At ₹40, buyers want 40 and sellers offer 80. What is the equilibrium price?
qa.e: At ₹30 a dozen, quantity demanded and quantity supplied are both 60 dozen.

qa.q: If the price in a market is above the equilibrium price, what happens?
qa.a: There is a surplus of goods
qa.e: Above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, so unsold goods pile up. That is a surplus.

qa.q: At ₹50 per kg, buyers want 40 kg of tomatoes but sellers offer 80 kg. How large is the surplus?
qa.a: 40 kg
qa.e: Surplus = quantity supplied − quantity demanded = 80 − 40 = 40 kg.

qa.q: Before Diwali, many more families want to buy sweets, while supply does not change. What happens to the price of sweets?
qa.a: It rises
qa.e: A rise in demand with the same supply creates a shortage at the old price, so the equilibrium price goes up.

qa.q: A bumper onion harvest brings far more onions to the mandi while demand stays the same. What happens to the price of onions?
qa.a: It falls
qa.e: A rise in supply with the same demand creates a surplus at the old price, so sellers lower the price.

qa.q: When there is a shortage (excess demand) in a market, what usually happens to the price?
qa.a: It rises
qa.e: When buyers want more than is available, they compete for the goods and sellers can raise the price until the shortage disappears.

qa.q: Every evening, a fruit seller is left with a big pile of unsold mangoes. What should he most likely do to sell them?
qa.a: Lower his price
qa.e: Unsold stock shows a surplus: his price is above equilibrium. Cutting the price will make buyers purchase more.

qa.q: What is a budget?
qa.a: A plan of expected income and spending for a period
qa.e: A budget plans how much money will come in and how it will be spent or saved over a week, month or year.

qa.q: Neha's family earns ₹30,000 a month and spends ₹27,500. What is their monthly surplus?
qa.e: Surplus = income − expenses = ₹30,000 − ₹27,500 = ₹2,500.

qa.q: When expenses are more than income, the budget is said to be:
qa.a: In deficit
qa.e: A deficit means spending is more than income, so the gap must be covered by savings or borrowing.

qa.q: Which of these is usually a fixed expense for a family?
qa.a: Monthly house rent
qa.e: Rent stays the same every month, so it is a fixed expense. Restaurant meals, gifts and electricity use change from month to month.

qa.q: Which of these is a need rather than a want?
qa.a: A medicine prescribed by a doctor
qa.e: Needs are things we must have to live safely and healthily, such as food, shelter, medicines and education.

qa.q: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
qa.a: Put aside savings as soon as you receive money, before spending
qa.e: Saving first makes sure savings actually happen, instead of saving only what is left at the end of the month.

qa.q: Aditya gets ₹1,500 pocket money a month. He spends ₹600 on snacks, ₹300 on mobile recharge and ₹400 on comics. How much is left for saving?
Why is it useful to track every expense for a month?
qa.a: It shows where money is being spent so you can cut waste
qa.e: Tracking reveals small 'leaks', such as frequent snacks, that add up. Then you can plan better.

qa.q: Raj saves ₹2,000 in a bank at 5% simple interest per year. How much interest does he earn in 3 years?
qa.e: Simple interest = 2,000 × 5 × 3 ÷ 100 = ₹300.

qa.q: ₹1,000 is deposited at 10% interest per year, compounded yearly. What is the amount after 2 years?
Why does money grow faster with compound interest than with simple interest at the same rate?
qa.a: Interest is also earned on the interest already added
qa.e: With compounding, each year's interest is added to the principal, so the next year's interest is calculated on a bigger amount.

qa.q: A school bag costs ₹200 this year. If its price rises by 10% in a year, what will it cost next year?
What happens to the purchasing power of ₹100 when there is inflation?
qa.a: It falls, because ₹100 buys fewer goods than before
qa.e: When prices rise, the same amount of money buys less. So inflation reduces purchasing power.

qa.q: What is the main purpose of an emergency fund?
qa.a: To pay for sudden needs like illness or urgent repairs
qa.e: An emergency fund protects a family from having to borrow when something unexpected happens.

qa.q: How is a fixed deposit different from a savings account?
qa.a: A fixed deposit keeps money for a fixed period and usually pays higher interest
qa.e: In a fixed deposit, money is locked for an agreed period, and in return the bank usually pays a higher rate than on a savings account.

qa.q: Tara and Vikram save the same amount every year at the same compound interest rate. Tara starts at 25 and Vikram at 35. Who is likely to have more at 60?
qa.a: Tara, because her money has more years to compound
qa.e: Tara saves for more years, and her money has 10 extra years to earn interest on interest. Starting early is a big advantage.

qa.q: A caller says he is from your bank and asks for the OTP sent to your phone to 'update your account'. What should you do?
qa.a: Refuse, end the call and inform a parent or the bank
qa.e: Banks never ask for OTPs. Sharing it could let the caller take money from the account.

qa.q: Your friend wants to send you ₹200 through UPI. What do you need to enter to receive it?
qa.a: Nothing; no PIN is needed to receive money
qa.e: You need a UPI PIN only to pay. A request asking you to enter your PIN to 'receive' money is a trick.

qa.q: Why is borrowing from a bank usually better than borrowing from an informal moneylender?
qa.a: Banks are regulated by the RBI and usually charge lower interest
qa.e: Formal lenders follow RBI rules and usually charge lower interest. Informal lenders may charge very high interest and are not regulated in the same way.

qa.q: Mr. Iyer borrows ₹10,000 from a bank at 12% simple interest for 1 year. How much must he repay in total at the end of the year?
What is an insurance premium?
qa.a: The regular amount paid to the insurer for cover
qa.e: You pay the premium regularly. In return, the insurance company pays you if an insured loss happens.

qa.q: Meena splits her savings between a fixed deposit, a recurring deposit and a little in other options. What is this called?
qa.a: Diversification
qa.e: Diversification spreads money across options, so a loss in one does not wipe out everything.

qa.q: A scheme promises to double your money in just one month with 'no risk'. What is the most sensible view?
qa.a: It is very likely a fraud, because high returns come with high risk
qa.e: Very high returns with no risk do not exist. Such promises are a common sign of a fraud.

qa.q: What is the national helpline number to report cyber financial fraud in India?
qa.e: 1930 is the national cyber fraud helpline. Reporting quickly gives the best chance of stopping the money from being taken away.

qa.q: Who is an entrepreneur?
qa.a: A person who spots an opportunity, organises resources and takes the risk of starting a business
qa.e: An entrepreneur identifies an opportunity, combines land, labour and capital, and bears the risk of the venture.

qa.q: What is the reward for the factor of production called entrepreneurship?
qa.a: Profit
qa.e: Profit is what the entrepreneur earns after paying for all the other factors. If costs are more than revenue, there is a loss instead.

qa.q: Which of these best describes a social entrepreneur?
qa.a: Someone who starts a venture mainly to solve a social problem, such as providing low-cost water filters in villages
qa.e: A social entrepreneur's main aim is to solve a problem in society, while also running the venture so it can continue.

qa.q: Meera's first snack stall failed. She studied what went wrong, changed her menu and opened again. Which quality does this show?
qa.a: Persistence
qa.e: Persistence means not giving up after failure, learning from mistakes and trying again.

qa.q: Why is entrepreneurship important for a country like India?
qa.a: It creates jobs and new products and helps the economy grow
qa.e: New enterprises hire workers, offer new goods and services and add to incomes, which helps the economy grow.

qa.q: What risk does an entrepreneur face?
qa.a: Losing the money invested if the business does not succeed
qa.e: Since the entrepreneur invests money and time without a guaranteed income, a failed business can mean a loss.

qa.q: Which factors of production does an entrepreneur bring together?
qa.a: Land, labour and capital
qa.e: The entrepreneur organises land (place), labour (workers) and capital (machines, tools, money) to produce goods or services.

qa.q: Ravi starts a small cycle-repair business and soon hires three helpers. What has he become?
qa.a: A job creator
qa.e: By starting a business and hiring others, Ravi has created jobs. Entrepreneurs are job creators.

qa.q: Which of these best describes a startup?
qa.a: A young business built on a new idea that aims to grow quickly
qa.e: Startups are new, built around an innovative idea and designed to grow and reach many customers.

qa.q: Why do founders build a minimum viable product (MVP) first?
qa.a: To test the idea with real users quickly and cheaply before spending a lot
qa.e: An MVP lets founders learn from real users early, so they can improve the product without wasting money.

qa.q: Kabir starts his app business using only his own savings, without loans or investors. What is this called?
qa.a: Bootstrapping
qa.e: Bootstrapping means funding a startup from your own savings and earnings.

qa.q: What is an angel investor?
qa.a: An individual who invests their own money in an early-stage startup, usually for a share of it
qa.e: Angel investors are individuals who back young startups with their own money, usually in exchange for equity.

qa.q: A startup sells millet laddoos at ₹80 a box. Each box costs ₹50 to make. If it sells 100 boxes, what profit does it make (ignoring other costs)?
qa.e: Profit per box = ₹80 − ₹50 = ₹30. For 100 boxes, profit = 100 × ₹30 = ₹3,000.

qa.q: Feedback shows that students do not want Priya's homework app, but teachers love it. She changes the app to serve teachers. What is this called?
qa.a: A pivot
qa.e: A pivot is a change in a startup's product or target customers, based on what founders learn from feedback.

qa.q: Before starting a cycle-rental service near a college in Pune, Aman surveys 200 students about whether they would use it. What is he doing?
qa.a: Market research
qa.e: Market research means collecting information about customers and the market to check whether there is real demand.

qa.q: An investor gives a startup ₹10 lakh in exchange for 10% equity. What does the investor get?
qa.a: A 10% share of ownership in the company
qa.e: Equity means part-ownership. The investor now owns 10% of the company and shares in its success or failure.

qa.q: What is the difference between an invention and an innovation?
qa.a: An invention creates something new, and an innovation puts a new idea to practical use
qa.e: Invention is about creating something new. Innovation is about turning ideas into products, services or processes that people use.

qa.q: Which legal right protects a new invention, such as a new machine?
qa.a: Patent
qa.e: A patent gives the inventor the exclusive right to make and sell the invention for a fixed period.

qa.q: For how many years does a patent protect an invention in India?
qa.e: In India, a patent lasts for 20 years from the date of filing. After that, others can use the invention freely.

qa.q: In which year was the Startup India initiative launched?
qa.e: The Government of India launched Startup India on 16 January 2016 to support and encourage new businesses.

qa.q: What is a 'unicorn' in the startup world?
qa.a: A startup valued at US$1 billion or more
qa.e: The term unicorn was used because such highly valued startups were once very rare.

qa.q: What does a startup incubator do?
qa.a: Helps early-stage startups with mentoring, workspace and contacts
qa.e: Incubators support young startups so their ideas can grow into working businesses.

qa.q: Which of these is the best example of frugal innovation?
qa.a: A clay fridge that keeps food cool without electricity
qa.e: Frugal innovation creates useful solutions at low cost with limited resources, like the clay fridge.

qa.q: A company wants to stop others from copying its brand name and logo. What should it register?
qa.a: A trademark
qa.e: Trademarks protect brand names, logos and symbols that identify a company's goods or services.
